chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Al-Nawfaly, from Al-Sakuni, from Ja'far, from his forefathers (peace be upon them), who said:
Whatever the tenth-part collector takes from you and throws into a jug, it is from your zakat; and whatever he does not throw into the jug, do not reckon it as your zakat.

key_terms.تَحْتَسِبْهُ: To reckon or count it (as valid)
key_terms.كُوزَةٍ: A jug or container (used as a symbol of official receipt)

ai.seo_question: How is the validity of zakat determined when collected by the government or ruler according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi provides a tangible legal criterion for validating tax payments to the Imam or ruling authority, emphasizing that the physical deposit into a designated container (kuz) serves as the definitive proof of fulfillment. It highlights the Shia scholarly focus on administrative transparency and the distinction between official dues and arbitrary exactions, ensuring that the taxpayer's obligation is discharged only when the amount is formally secured by the authority.

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim, from Al Nowfaly, from Al Sakuny, 
(It has been narrated) from Ja’far<sup>asws</sup>, from his<sup>asws</sup> forefathers<sup>asws</sup> having said:
‘Whatever the tax collector (of 10%) takes from you and throws it into a jug, so it is from your Zakāt, and whatever he does not throw in into the jug, so you cannot reckon it to be from your Zakāt’.
en.sarwar: 6. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from al-Nawfaliy from al-Sakuniy who has said the following: “Abu Ja‘far, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, has narrated from his ancestor, ‘Alayhim al-Salam, this Hadith.
‘Whatever the collector of one out of ten (Zakat collector) charges you and deposits it in the mug (the safe), it is your Zakat. If he does not do so then do not count it as your Zakat.’”
